query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the content of zirconium (Zr) and hafnium (Hf) in the high-entropy boride matrix improves resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion in boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components with a standard high-entropy boride composition that has lower levels of Zr and Hf.
generation.intervention: Doping the boride material with additional Zr and Hf during the processing to achieve an elevated concentration in the matrix.
generation.conditions: Under high-temperature molten-aluminum exposure conditions typical of hot-dip aluminum plating, processed via spark plasma sintering around 2000 °C, and in environments where oxidation is a potential concern.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a single-phase hexagonal high-entropy boride structure enriched with Zr and Hf, which has been shown in gas-dynamic tests to enhance thermal-oxidative resistance.
generation.mechanism: The increased Zr and Hf content promotes a more stable and protective oxide layer and compositional uniformity that resists permeation by molten aluminum, thereby reducing corrosion rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified component will demonstrate significantly higher resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion, as measured by lower mass loss and reduced interface degradation compared to components with lower Zr/Hf content.
generation.baseline: Performance of conventional boride-based components with standard (lower) levels of Zr and Hf under identical molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be valid when processing methods (e.g., spark plasma sintering at approximately 2000 °C) yield a homogeneous high-entropy boride phase; deviations in phase composition or significant impurities may negate the corrosion resistance benefit.
generation.uncertainty: While gas-dynamic tests indicate improved thermal-oxidative resistance with increased Zr and Hf, it is uncertain if these improvements directly translate to enhanced resistance against molten-aluminum corrosion. Further targeted experimental validation is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy boride specimens: one with the baseline (lower Zr and Hf content) and one with increased Zr and Hf content. Expose both sets to a controlled molten-aluminum environment that replicates the operational conditions in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment for a set duration.
measurements: Mass loss measurements before and after exposure
Analysis of the corrosion depth and interfacial degradation using microscopy
Phase composition analysis through X-ray diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens with increased Zr and Hf content do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in metrics (lower mass loss, reduced corrosion depth, maintained microhardness, and stable phase composition) compared to baseline specimens, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
This manuscript shows the study of the structure, mechanical, and chemical properties of high-entropy borides MeB2 (Me = Ti, Ta, Nb, Hf, Zr). High-entropy borides were synthesized by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. A chemically homogeneous powder with a low iron content (0.12%) was obtained in a planetary mill by rotating the planetary disk/pots at 200–400 rpm and a processing time of 7.5 h. The structure, mechanical, and chemical properties of the resulting high-entropy borides have been studied. A single-phase hexagonal structure is formed during spark plasma sintering of mechanically alloyed powders at 2000 °C. The microhardness of the samples ranged from 1763 to 1959 HV. Gas-dynamic tests of the synthesized materials showed that an increase in the content of Zr and Hf in the composition increases the thermal-oxidative resistance of the material.
